item.title: The call for an agentic standard: We need to stop shipping the same form four different times
item.description: One description, four renderers. That is the whole argument in a picture.Every assistant draws its own way, and the bill lands on the people who already maintain your button component. This is a call to arms to fix this.Connecting was the easy part and the plumbing is close to settled for MCP Servers, which followed the lead of HTTP dressed up for the AI era.What isn’t is what each client does when your agent needs a date picker on screen: which components exist, who owns the rendering, what it looks like when it shows up on a screen.There are four ways a client can do it, and every product you care about sits in one of them. Nobody publishes that comparison, so sorting out which client does which took four specifications, a protocol proposal and a Google engineering post, and none of them agree on what to call any of it.Google’s trying to create that standard — A2UI. It’s short for agent-to-UI, their attempt at a shared approach i.e. doing the right thing.Introduced in December 2025, it is declarative: the agent sends JSON naming components the client already holds in a catalog, and the client draws them in its own code. No markup crosses the wire, and no styling either.Version 1.0 is still a release candidate and it looks a lot like the HTML constructs of 1999. It matters because it is the one proposal on the table that no vendor “owns.”Working this out should not be a research project, and this is a call to arms to get there.Here’s where we are today with A2UI and its adoption.A2UIDeclarative JSON, rendered by the clientThe agent names components the client already holds, and nobody owns the vocabulary. Three apps render it without a bundled renderer, which means they are hedging their bets.Google Gemini Enterprise renders the standard A2UI component set. Styling is Google’s.Google Opal draws its natural-language mini-apps with it. Styling is Opal’s.OpenClaw Canvas renders agent-built UI on connected devices. Styling belongs to the plugin.A developer tier renders it too — Google’s ADK Web, the alpha Flutter GenUI SDK, CopilotKit AG-UI, Vercel json-render — but nobody works there.Claude and ChatGPT support something that looks the same, and it’s really an IFRAME into their clients.Sandboxed HTML, if you ship the A2UI renderer yourselfA page arrives and runs in a frame. More expressive, less governable, and it stays a web object wherever it lands. These clients do render A2UI: the server sends application/a2ui+json and the app parses it locally with a bundled renderer, which means they are also hedging their bets. Google published three patterns for combining the two in June 2026.OpenAI ChatGPT renders app UI through the Apps SDK. Styling is yours — you shipped the CSS.Anthropic Claude renders Artifacts and hosts MCP Apps carrying their own renderer. Styling is yours, same reason.Not A2UI ListSlack supports a BlockKit version.Declarative JSON through vendor catalogSame mechanism, one owner.Microsoft Teams and Outlook render Adaptive Cards across seven renderer SDKs. Styling is Microsoft’s, set by host config.Salesforce Slack renders Block Kit. Styling is Slack’s — its docs say Slack controls contrast so you don’t have to.Consumer Google Gemini doesn’t support anything at all.Generated code or nothingThe model writes the interface fresh each time, or the client has no surface at all.Google Gemini Consumer, writes generative UI per prompt. Styling is whatever the model invented that minute, if at all.xAI Grok renders nothing. It has tools and no surface format at all.The only approach that lets your server control appearance is the one that ships a page, and that’s the one that turns into a webview on a phone. Every declarative option hands styling to the client, which is a feature right up until the client belongs to somebody else.Two more things fall out.The declarative approaches are one mechanism with different owners, which is why the model was never the argument.A2UI reaches the clients your users actually open only by shipping its renderer inside every payload — the adapter tax in miniature, and a strange thing to call a standard.You will pay for that gap. Not in licensing — in a tax. Every surface is another target your design system has to serve, and every platform multiplies it again.Surfaces times platforms — that’s the surface tax.The web spent five years rendering everything twice because nobody could agree on a target.Learn from the browser warsNetscape and Microsoft spent the late 1990s shipping tags at each other. document.layers against document.all.Every serious site carried browser-sniffing code at the top and two layouts underneath, and the people who wrote that code hated it. Ask Jeffrey Zeldman, which I covered in this article — Designing with web standards: The playbook for this AI moment.Then Internet Explorer 6 won and the web stopped moving for five years. Firefox pulled developers back by rendering to spec. Google Chrome arrived in 2008 and finished the job — fast, yes, but mostly predictable. You could write a page once and know what it would do. Chrome now holds close to 68% of the browser market, per Statcounter’s July 2026 figures, so it’s a solved problem.Agentic UI are the old browsers in a new costume, and they are called ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot and Slack, with a side of Grok and Perplexity.The authors of MCP Apps, an extension to the Model Context Protocol, say so in their proposal — without a standard, “developers must maintain separate implementations or adapters for different hosts.” MCP-UI, the project that spec grew out of, counts Postman, Hugging Face, Shopify and ElevenLabs among its adopters. The adapters exist.Someone is paying for them — it’s us.Chat is a solved shape. The canvas is where the cost lives.Look past chat to the canvasA message list with an input and a stop button is a solved shape, drawn about the same way everywhere. The canvas is where it gets expensive — Gemini’s Dynamic View, ChatGPT’s Canvas, Microsoft rendering app UI in Copilot chat and out into Teams, Outlook, Word and Excel.In Google’s own November 2025 evaluation of that generated UI, sites built by human experts still came out on top, and generation can take “a minute or more.”Runtime assembly needs a shared parts list. Right now every vendor keeps their own.So Google runs both approaches at once — open-ended code generation in the consumer app, a declarative catalog in the protocol. A consumer canvas can afford a minute and a look it invented this morning. Your product cannot. An approval form on your canvas has to be your date picker, your error states, your empty state, and it has to land before the user’s attention does.Two working formats, a decade of production traffic, and neither one is neutral.Copy what Slack and Microsoft already provedThe standards argument keeps skipping this. It was solved twice already, in production, by companies with no idea they were prototyping agent UI.Slack’s Block Kit is blocks, block elements and composition objects, authored as JSON. A server sends the structure; Slack draws it. It runs across messages, modals and App Home tabs, with limits that tell you it’s a real system under load — 50 blocks per message, 100 in a modal.Microsoft’s Adaptive Cards went further. The pitch is nearly word for word what A2UI now promises: “platform-agnostic snippets of UI, authored in JSON, that apps and services can openly exchange.” Microsoft maintains seven renderer SDKs — JavaScript, .NET, .NET WPF, .NET HTML, Windows UWP, Android and iOS — with React Native contributed by the community.Teams alone documents a whole card taxonomy: hero, thumbnail, list, connector, adaptive in the same way design systems are documented.Nobody has to prove declarative UI works across native clients. Microsoft shipped that proof years ago.The model is not the risk.The problem is ownership. Block Kit draws in Slack. Adaptive Cards draw in Microsoft’s products. Both are proprietary, and neither will ever be the format the other adopts. If you have ever fought a Block Kit layout into your brand, you know the ceiling of a parts bin somebody else owns.A catalog you approved once, against a page you have to trust every time.Make the baseline neutralA2UI is that baseline, or the best attempt so far. Its 1.0 specification defines surfaces, components and catalogs as JSON naming parts the client already holds — Google calls it a “declarative data format, not executable code.” Same shape as an Adaptive Card, except no vendor owns the parts bin and it streams, so the interface builds as the agent thinks.Compare that to the other direction. MCP Apps delivers text/html;profile=mcp-app into a sandboxed iframe. That's a page, not a description, and it never becomes a SwiftUI sheet or a Jetpack Compose bottom sheet — on a phone you get a webview, with the wrong scroll physics, the wrong keyboard, Dynamic Type ignored and a VoiceOver reading order from a different document than the one around it. Bundling an A2UI renderer inside that page gets the vocabulary back, not the native widgets.A component that doesn’t exist in your system cannot appear at all.The declarative side inverts all of that. A component that doesn’t exist in your system cannot appear at all, an easier promise to make to a security team than “the sandbox will hold.” A2UI’s community renderer list covers SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose, React Native, Vue and Lynx — the same native-renderer play Adaptive Cards made, minus the owner.Version 1.0 stripped theme properties out of the payload entirely, so a button carries a primary variant and nothing about color. Christine Vallaure's UX Collective piece puts the designer's half plainly: the intelligence decides what to show, your design system decides what it looks like. That holds only where the catalog is yours.The caveat: most of those mobile renderers are volunteer work, and A2UI’s documentation tells you to check compatibility yourself. Microsoft staffs seven of its eight.Surfaces times platforms. The same date picker, specified and built over and over.Add up the surface taxDo the multiplication: Your design system probably serves the web, iOS and Android today. Add ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot across Teams and Outlook, and Slack.Ten surfaces across three platforms isn’t 10 problems, it’s the same date picker in Block Kit JSON, again as an Adaptive Card, again for whatever ChatGPT wants, then regression-tested against a matrix nobody staffed.There’s a rough price on this for mobile already.A 2026 survey of 267 app development companies by GoodFirms put a mid-level product built natively for iOS and Android at $120,000 to $300,000, against 20% to 40% less to build it once cross-platform, and maintenance adds 15% to 25% of budget every year after. Agent surfaces cost less per unit, but the shape is the same, and you’re adding units faster than you ever added platforms.It isn’t elegance. It’s who absorbs the complexity, and right now the answer is your design systems team, if you even have one of at all.Nathan Curtis wrote about balancing platforms in a design system at EightShapes: once a system serves more than one platform, the real work is deciding what’s shared and what’s justifiably different.Agent surfaces add a twist — you don’t own the renderer, so you can’t decide at all. The cost lands in the drift. Sparkbox’s 2022 design systems survey of 219 practitioners found 37% of maintainers struggling with design-code parity and 16% tracking usage metrics, and that was before AI.One shared format doesn’t delete the work.It changes what you maintain from N implementations to one catalog with N renderers, and moves that burden onto the platform vendors, and right now that’s your team.Pick a targetAfter all of this, A2UI might not be the one, in same way there were competing standards in 1999.Version 1.0 is still a release candidate, the repository has no neutral foundation behind it, and every native deployment so far is Google’s own. Google has abandoned better-supported things.But the shape is right, and we know it because two companies already shipped it. Adaptive Cards proved a JSON card renders as native UI across seven renderer SDKs. Block Kit proved it carries real interaction at scale. Neither can be the standard, because a standard owned by Microsoft is Microsoft’s standard.So pick your target, and make every vendor answer one question before you build against theirs: which renderers do you ship, on which devices and who maintains them. The ones who can’t answer are asking you to pay the tax for them.Start with these four moves now and then plan for a new worldCount the cells, not the surfaces. Put surfaces down one axis and platforms across the other, then fill in who owns each cell today. The empty cells are your roadmap, and the count turns this into a budget line.Write the catalog, not the screens. Pick the 12 components an agent needs to finish a task in your product — table, form, date picker, confirmation, status, error and empty state — and specify each with its states and constraints, versioned. That asset transfers to whichever format wins. Screens built against one vendor’s surface don’t.Read the Adaptive Cards schema before you design anything. It’s the most mature declarative UI vocabulary in production, and it will tell you in an afternoon which of your components survive translation and which only work because you control the CSS.Test on a mid-range Android phone first, not last. Run your first agent-rendered form on real hardware with TalkBack on and Dynamic Type up. If it only holds together in a desktop browser, you’ve found the ceiling.The call for an agentic standard: We need to stop shipping the same form four different times was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Design has outgrown the traditional designer
item.description: Why design education must reconsider the kind of student it imagines.Photo by shraga kopstein on UnsplashFor decades, design offered artistically inclined students an appealing compromise. They could pursue a practical career without giving up creativity. Someone with visual talent learned typography, composition, color, image-making, and a collection of professional tools. With enough skill, that student could turn artistic ability into commercial work without the uncertainty of pursuing a career as a traditional artist.That understanding of the designer still influences recruitment and what many aspiring designers expect from the profession. Design is often presented as a field where creative people can produce visually compelling work while building a recognizable career. The appeal is understandable, and generations of exceptional designers entered the profession through exactly that route.I know this because it’s how my journey began, as it did for countless others. I was good at drawing, interested in art, and attracted to a profession that offered a practical outlet for my creativity. That foundation served me well, but it would not have been enough for the career I eventually built.As the profession changed, I learned to code, moved into user experience and interface design, honed my strategic and business thinking, and developed an interest in the ethical and theoretical questions raised by technology. My career evolved because I did not remain confined by the traditional designer persona.After two decades in professional design and now as a design educator, I see a growing mismatch between that persona and the profession students are preparing to enter. Students who are comfortable producing visual work are not always interested in research, systems, ethics, technology, or the reasoning that precedes a design decision. Those subjects can feel secondary to the creative work they expected to do, even though designers are now routinely responsible for them.Artistically inclined students still have a place in design, and replacing them with technically inclined students would solve nothing. Likewise, coding ability, business knowledge, or analytical skill does not automatically produce a good designer. What matters is whether students are curious about the questions that now surround the artifact, including how it functions, whose interests it serves, and what consequences it produces.It is easy to point the finger at AI, but the profession’s transformation began much earlier — AI has simply made it more visible. Designers increasingly work on digital products that require attention to behavior, navigation, accessibility, technical constraints, business goals, and decisions affecting entire systems. While traditional design has always involved solving problems, the scope of those problems and the designer’s responsibility for addressing them have expanded.Labor data offers one practical indication of where the profession is moving. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment for graphic designers to decline 2 percent between 2025 and 2035, while employment for web and digital interface designers is projected to grow 6 percent. The agency also expects automated tools, including AI, to make graphic designers more productive and reduce the number of workers needed.In 2025, the median annual wage for graphic designers was $62,960, compared with $104,000 for web and digital interface designers. Technology-sector salaries may account for part of the difference, but the market's direction is clear. Employers are paying more for designers who can work with digital products, technical systems, user behavior, and product strategy than for those whose expertise is primarily visual. Traditional visual skills still have value, but they no longer command the same demand or economic value on their own.Hiring research reported by Figma reinforces this broader shift. While visual polish remained important to 58 percent of hiring managers, it was only one capability within a much wider profile. More than 45 percent also identified collaboration, systems thinking, and product strategy as critical, while 73 percent reported increasing demand for proficiency with AI tools and 79 percent for knowledge of AI product design. Employers are not abandoning visual craft. They are seeking designers whose visual ability is joined with technical, strategic, and systemic knowledge.I see the mismatch most clearly when students reach the parts of a project that precede the visual work. They may be eager to design screens but impatient with research, resistant to technical constraints, or inclined to treat strategy as documentation to complete before the real design begins. Technology is sometimes learned well enough to operate but not well enough to question.These reactions are not simply failures of effort. Many students entered the field expecting a professional outlet for artistic creativity. A discipline increasingly concerned with behavior, systems, evidence, and consequences can feel like a change in the terms of that promise.Changing the curriculum without changing the recruitment pitch leaves that mismatch intact. Programs that present design primarily as a practical outlet for creativity will attract students who expect creative expression to organize the profession. Their frustration is understandable when the education they encounter differs from the career they were promised.Design programs should therefore reconsider what they advertise and what they evaluate during admissions. A visual portfolio can remain part of the process without serving as the only meaningful evidence of potential. Applicants could also explain how they understood a problem, considered conflicting needs, or changed a decision after encountering new evidence. An imperfect artifact supported by thoughtful reasoning may reveal more than a polished portfolio organized around personal style.Recruitment could also extend beyond students who already identify with art. Future designers may come through psychology, computer science, business, sociology, communication, or philosophy because they are interested in behavior, technology, organizations, culture, or ethics. Their entry would expand the design field's capabilities rather than displace its artistic students.The same shift should appear in teaching and evaluation. Projects could require students to defend consequential decisions rather than merely present finished work. Critiques could examine how they responded to conflicting user, technical, and organizational needs. Capstone projects could include evidence of research, iteration, ethical reasoning, and collaboration alongside the final artifact. This would not diminish visual craft, but it would place craft within the broader judgment contemporary design requires.The profession needs people who can understand consequences not visible in the final artifact. For example, decisions that make an interface simpler, faster, or more personalized may also transfer control from its user to the system behind it. Designers must understand whose interests those systems represent and what users give up for convenience. Such consequences cannot be judged by looking at the screen alone.This type of responsibility also explains why design will survive AI—despite all the doom and gloom. Generative systems can produce graphics, layouts, interfaces, and variations with extraordinary speed, reducing the number of people needed for visual production. But producing possibilities is not the same as determining which are worth pursuing. Organizations will still need designers to define the purpose, decide whose needs take priority, evaluate consequences, and accept responsibility for the result.In this new landscape, creativity also takes on a broader meaning. It can appear in framing a problem, exposing a hidden assumption, reorganizing a system, or deciding not to build a proposed product. A beautiful design artifact may demonstrate exceptional craft while serving a system that should never have existed.Designers whose primary value comes from operating tools and producing polished artifacts will increasingly compete with systems capable of doing that work. Those who can interpret complex situations, make defensible decisions, work across disciplines, and direct those systems toward worthwhile purposes occupy a less replaceable position.The future of design education depends on more than revised courses, certificates, and new software. Programs must reconsider the person they imagine when they describe a future designer. Artistic imagination remains valuable, but it must be joined by curiosity about research, technology, systems, and the consequences of design decisions.Design education should continue to welcome students who love making beautiful things. But it must stop implying that this desire alone defines a designer. The profession’s future belongs to people who are curious about emerging technologies, willing to adapt as the field changes, and capable of determining not only what can be made, but what should be made, whom it serves, and what it sets in motion.Don’t miss out! Join my email list and receive the latest content.Design has outgrown the traditional designer was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: You can’t grow roses in a cornfield
item.description: A conversation with Whitney Hess, on careers, whispers, and where to plant yourselfPhoto by Bob Bowie on UnsplashSome questions sound administrative but are not, and “why do you want to switch jobs?” turns out to be one of them. I asked it on a mentoring call in the way you would ask about notice periods or portfolio order, one practical item among several, and the designer on my screen began to cry. Neither of us expected it. We sat with it for a moment, the way you do when a video call suddenly contains something real, and when she tried to answer, the answer had very little to do with jobs.I brought this moment to Whitney Hess, who spent a decade as one of the most visible independent UX consultants of that era, based in New York for much of it with clients around the world, before consciously shifting her business from consulting to coaching, and who has therefore listened to more designers talk about their careers than almost anyone alive. She was not surprised. Long before people can say out loud that the work no longer fits, she told me, they hear it as a whisper: a quiet, dismissible sense that this is not what they want. The whisper is patient. Left unanswered it does not fade but grows, until one day it has become a daily shout, and a person finds herself crying on an ordinary mentoring call without quite knowing how she got there.Whitney HessI have been interviewing designers who left the craft, or reshaped it into something new, for a book I am slowly writing about what is happening to our profession. Whitney is firmly in the second camp, and she will correct you if you suggest otherwise: she has never left UX, and she keeps her identity as a UX designer today. What she changed was the shape of the work, and she changed it while everything was still going up: the clients were blue-chip, the blog was widely read, the field itself was ascendant. That is what makes her worth listening to now. Most of us only examine what we really want when circumstances force the question, and she examined it voluntarily, at the height of a thriving practice, while the whisper was still at whisper volume. Since it is the quiet season, and half the industry is out of office with more time to think than usual, her story seems worth telling at length.What the whisper actually saysWhitney’s move out of consulting was not a leap, and it did not begin with dissatisfaction. She registered her company in 2005, went fully independent about three years later, and built the kind of practice most designers would consider a destination: Scientific American, WNYC, the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. The trouble, when it arrived, arrived inside the work rather than around it. “I wasn’t really addressing the systemic problems” she told me. A project would end, the deliverable would be good, and the organization that received it would remain exactly the organization it had been before. So she began pulling her clients’ own teams deeper into the work, partly for better outcomes and partly because, as she put it, it “felt weird not leaving the company in a better place.”It is worth noticing what the whisper was actually saying, because it was not saying quit; it was saying something more precise. It was telling her which part of the work was hers: less the solving than the facilitating, less the deliverable than the people gathered around it. The signs were public long before she acted on them. In 2012 she wrote on her blog that her consulting role had become “kind of like that of a group-therapist,” which reads today like a diagnosis published in plain sight; within eight months of writing it she had enrolled in a yearlong coaching training. The certification did not change what she was. It caught up with what she had already become.The biggest challenge is how you design your career.The economics of listeningThe economics deserve to be told plainly, because this is the part that career-change stories usually leave out, and because Whitney, it turns out, has crossed twice.The first crossing was the raw one. In 2008, after three years of running her consulting business on the side, she left her full-time job to make it her whole livelihood, and the numbers underneath that decision were thin: about three months of savings, in New York, with no institutional net. “It was terrifying,” she told me, and she meant it concretely enough that she had decided she would work at Starbucks if that was what staying independent required. What she had instead of a cushion was a track record of a particular kind. “I’ve always trusted my ability to figure it out,” she said. “I knew I was going to be resourceful.” Designers will recognize that sentence, because it describes the psychological posture of every project we have ever started: a new domain, unclear requirements, stakeholders we have never met, and a working assumption that within a few weeks we will understand the problem better than the people who handed it to us. It is a strange kind of confidence, empirical rather than temperamental, assembled from having been dropped into the unknown many times and having found the shape of it each time. Whitney’s real innovation was pointing that confidence at her own livelihood.The second crossing, into coaching in 2013 and 2014, looked nothing like the first, and the difference is the lesson. By then she had significantly more savings, and she kept taking UX consulting projects while the coaching practice ramped up, winding one income down as the other grew. The first crossing she survived on nerve; the second she designed. In time the coaching revenue found its footing, and the consulting decade turned out not to be a sunk cost at all. Those years were what allowed her to sit credibly across from the senior leaders she now coaches, which is to say the practice she wound down kept working for her inside the practice she built.The people who arriveIt would be easy to file what Whitney does now under career services, and the label would miss most of it. People rarely bring a career to a coach because everything is fine, and the field she serves keeps producing a particular kind of trouble. It is full of accidental leaders, she observes: craft people promoted into managing others because that was the only ladder on offer, now spending their days in meetings, mourning the work their hands used to do. Designers at large, she has noticed, see themselves as problem solvers and business growers and are received as people who make nice things, and they extend endless empathy to their users and almost none to their own kind, or to themselves. “We take a lot of responsibility on our shoulders,” she said of her profession.So the coaching rarely stays inside the career, because the career is rarely where the trouble actually lives. Her question for clients is not what the next role should be but something quieter and harder: what is their best self, and what would work look like if it were built around it? It is the same instinct that surfaced in her consulting days, the group-therapist tendency she once joked about on her blog, matured into the job itself. It also explains her list of interests better than any career-services framing could. A coach who follows her clients’ troubles all the way down will end up talking about money, about grief, about what remains when the title is gone, which is to say she ends up coaching a life, and the career only as the part of it that happens between nine and five.In defence of detoursThe part of our conversation I have thought about most came when I asked what is next for her. Instead of an answer about deepening the coaching practice, she gave me a list: she is interested in financial advising, in training as an end-of-life doula, and, she added with a smile, in private investigation.The list sounds eccentric until you trace where each item comes from. The interest in finance grew out of twenty years of running her own business, and out of the money questions her clients keep carrying into sessions, since you cannot coach someone about their career for very long without talking about what the career is for. The doula interest grew out of grief. She lost a few people close to her in recent years, accompanying those endings at close range, and emerged knowing something she could offer other people in the hardest passage of their lives. Even the private investigator idea, the one that made us both laugh, is her day job wearing a trench coat: she is paid to read systems, incentives, and decision makers, and to notice what everyone in the room is leaving unsaid.None of these are exits, in other words. They are continuations, experiences she already owns waiting for a context that wants them. Underneath them sits a view of careers that is quietly radical: a working life is not a ladder within one profession but a body of accumulated experience that can be recombined, more than once, into new work. “The decisions that we make now become the legacy that we leave,” she said at one point, and the word legacy is doing real work in that sentence. She thinks about careers on the scale of a whole life, endings included, which may be why becoming a doula does not strike her as a change of subject.Held up to that light, your own history gets interesting quickly. The banking designer who has spent five years inside compliance reviews is, whether she thinks of it this way or not, becoming an expert in regulated systems. The design lead who has survived three reorganizations has learned things about organizations that consultants charge for. We rarely see this in ourselves, because we are looking at our job titles, and a job title is a summary written by someone else, for a purpose that was never ours.Where you plant yourselfNone of this means growth is purely a matter of will, and the sentence that gave this piece its title was about the limits of it. “You can’t grow roses in a cornfield” Whitney said. Your ability to grow depends to an uncomfortable degree on the environment you are planted in. A cornfield is not hostile; it is optimized for corn. An organization that understands design as decoration will not, through any effort of yours, come to understand it as systems thinking, and the career path available to you inside any company is a function of how mature its design practice is, rather than of what your ambition deserves. Careers, in her telling, transfer no better than components do. “You cannot design one widget and expect it to work in every app in the app store,” she said.The biggest decision they need to make is where they plant themselves.Her practical advice follows from the metaphor. “The biggest decision they need to make is where they plant themselves,” she said of the designers she coaches, and she talks about that decision the way people talk about buying property: “I wouldn’t buy a house without doing my research on the neighborhood.” Designers, meanwhile, routinely join companies knowing less about the design culture than they would insist on knowing about a place they were going to live. Who does design report to? What happened to the last three senior designers? Does the career ladder exist anywhere outside the recruiting deck, and has anyone actually climbed it? These are questions you can ask in an interview, and asking them tells the company something about you that works in your favor.Speaking as someone who runs a design team inside a large bank, I can confirm the information is not hidden. People will tell you how design really lives in their organization, sometimes proudly, sometimes bitterly, usually within ten minutes. We run more discovery for a two-week feature than most of us run for a five-year employment decision, and there is no good reason for that asymmetry.Running discovery on yourselfWhat I take from Whitney’s story, and what I would like to hand to the designer from my mentoring call and to everyone quietly carrying some version of her whisper, is not reassurance. The market is hard at the entry level, unstable in the middle, and strange at the top, and reassurance would be a kind of lie. What her story offers instead is a method, and it is one designers already practice daily on other people’s problems.It begins with discovery, pointed inward. The research question is not which job titles you could plausibly get. It is which moments of the past five years felt like yours, and what people keep bringing to you that appears nowhere in your job description. Whitney’s whisper named the facilitator inside the problem solver. Yours is likely to be similarly specific, if you give it the kind of patient attention you would give a user interview.It continues with an inventory. Somewhere in your history is experience that feels off-topic: the failed side business, the caregiving years, the community you moderate, the domain you absorbed by accident. On the ladder model of a career this is clutter. On Whitney’s model it is material, and some of it is closer to becoming work than you think.Then comes the audit of the soil, which is the uncomfortable step, because it can return the finding that nothing is wrong with you while something is wrong with the field you are planted in. The move that follows is not necessarily out of design. Sometimes it is only out of the cornfield.And then you prototype, cheaply and early, the way she did both times. The consulting business ran for three years on the side before she trusted it with her livelihood, and the coaching practice ramped up while consulting still paid the bills. The jumps were real, but each was the last step of a long prototype rather than the first step of a plan. Mentoring one person, taking one course, writing one essay: these are the paper prototypes of a next career, and they cost about as much as paper.What holds it together is the kickoff feeling, that trained confidence in your own resourcefulness. It is not Whitney’s private gift. It belongs to the profession, built into all of us by every project that started in fog and ended in shipping. UX has always attracted people who want their work to mean something, and that appetite survives any particular job, which is exactly why it aches when the job stops feeding it.A question for a slow afternoonNear the end of our call Whitney said she wants to keep developing her skills “over the arc of my career,” and it was clear she meant the arc of a working life, forty-some years across however many professions those years turn out to contain. She likes variety, she told me: “I like having every day feel different.” “Life happens,” she reminded me. “All your life plans go out the window. Covid happens.” What survives is the why underneath, the boundaries you will not trade away, and a flexibility about nearly everything else, so that when an opening appears you are able to recognize it and move.We need to be connected with our WHY.I think about my mentee often. The tears were not a breakdown, as far as I can tell. They were information arriving, a whisper that had been ignored long enough to find another channel, and the kindest thing that moment did was make the question impossible to postpone any further.So, in the spirit of the season, and with whatever slow afternoon you can find: what do you actually love doing? Not what you are good at, which is a different list, and not what pays, which is a third. If you trusted yourself the way you trust yourself at every kickoff, what would you scope first? Somewhere inside the job you have is the work you want, and finding it is not a leap of faith. It is a design problem, and you have been training for it your whole career.Whitney Hess coaches creative leaders at whitneyhess.com. Her 2012 essay “Designing the Company, Not the Product” is where this story quietly begins.This conversation is part of a series of interviews with designers who left the craft or reshaped it into something new, for a book in progress.If the soil audit above left you wondering where you actually stand, I built a tool for that step: a free, scenario based self assessment, about ten minutes, and the output is a profile, not a grade. Treat it as a private room. You can take it at designlevel.io/assessmentAnd if you think I am wrong about any of this, tell me. The strongest corrections to my thinking have come from readers.You can’t grow roses in a cornfield was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: UX in 2027 may be less about interfaces and more about behavior
item.description: The signals I see today point to more adaptive interfaces, more delegated actions, and a larger responsibility for designers to define the limitsFrom fixed interfaces to adaptive systems: UX increasingly defines how software interprets, responds, and acts. Image generated with AI by OpenAI, art-directed by Lucas Camara.The most important change in UX may not be visible on a screen.Software is beginning to interpret goals, assemble interfaces, choose tools, and act on a person’s behalf. Google Search can now generate interactive graphs, simulations, and mini apps in response to a query. Google’s A2UI project lets agents compose interfaces from trusted component catalogs. Gartner expects task-specific agents to appear in 40% of enterprise applications by the end of 2026.None of those signals proves what UX will look like in 2027. Together, however, they point to a shift in the object we design. A fixed flow describes what a person can do. An adaptive system must also define what the product can infer, generate, and do for that person.My own use of AI is much less dramatic than the demos. I use it to organize information, recover details from transcripts, prepare placeholder copy, name layers, connect variables, and explore product data. In a financial organization, confidentiality and internal policy sharply limit where experimentation is appropriate. That gap between public capability and responsible use is not incidental. It is part of the design problem.This is not a prediction that interfaces will disappear. It is an evidence-based hypothesis: if software takes on more decisions and actions, UX will need to spend more of its craft defining behavior, limits, and ways to return control.The interface is not disappearing, but it may stop telling the whole storyTraditional software waits for a sequence of instructions. Agentic software is designed to interpret a goal, plan steps, use tools, and return with a result.That changes what an interface needs to do. I can make this concrete with two ERP products I worked on earlier in my career. AppHealth had to be modernized and standardized across an ecosystem that included financial and management operations. AzulControle also concentrated operational rules, records, and reports in a conventional ERP structure.Consider one recurring management task: understanding why the financial result for a period changed. In a fixed ERP, the manager first chooses a company or unit, selects a date range, opens a financial report, applies categories and status filters, compares the result with another period, and often exports the data to assemble an explanation elsewhere. Each step may be valid, but the system asks the person to translate a business question into its information architecture.An intent-based version could begin with: “Why did this unit’s result fall compared with last month?” The system could identify the relevant period and unit, compare revenue and expense categories, surface the largest variations, and compose a chart for that question.The interface would not end there. Before the analysis could support a decision, it would need to show which records were included, which definition of “result” it used, whether any data was missing, and how the comparison was calculated. If the manager asks the system to act, such as changing a forecast or approving a payment, permissions, confirmation, and a reversible record become mandatory.This example changes the flow from navigation by system structure to navigation by intent. It does not eliminate the ERP’s complexity. It relocates some of that complexity into interpretation, where mistakes can be harder to notice.These figures show how quickly companies are experimenting with agentic AI. They also make cost, business value, and risk controls increasingly important when deciding where greater autonomy is actually useful.From fixed flows to constrained adaptationGenerative UI is often described as an interface created or adapted according to a person’s goal and context. Nielsen Norman Group connects the idea to outcome-oriented design, in which the experience focuses more directly on the user’s desired result.We already see small versions of this when an AI conversation produces buttons, checkboxes, tables, or other controls instead of asking the user to type everything. The important part is not that AI can generate a button. It is that the system is beginning to choose which interaction makes sense at that moment.Google is already testing a more literal version of this idea. Its 2026 Search announcements describe generative interfaces that build custom graphs, trackers, dashboards, simulations, and mini apps for a query. Google Research reported that people strongly preferred its generative UI prototypes to baseline language-model responses, while interfaces built by experts still received the highest ratings. The signal is meaningful, but so is the limitation: generation improved the response without replacing design expertise.Google Search generates an interactive interface tailored to a specific question. Image: Google.By 2027, more interfaces may behave like temporary explanations of what the system understood, what it recommends, and what it still needs from the user.I do not think this will make fixed interfaces obsolete. Stable structures support learning, spatial memory, predictability, and confidence. These qualities matter even more in healthcare, finance, government, and enterprise products, where a vague status or misunderstood permission can affect an entire operation.The useful direction, in my view, is not unlimited personalization. It is constrained adaptation. The system can respond to context, but inside boundaries defined by accessibility, business rules, permissions, consistency, and risk.This is also why UX cannot become a recipe executed by an agent. What works for one audience, product, or operational context may fail in another. The difficult part is noticing those differences.When software starts acting, trust becomes part of the interactionThere is enough movement around agents to take them seriously. Gartner projected that up to 40% of enterprise applications would include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, compared with less than 5% in 2025.The counter-signal is equally important. Gartner also forecast that more than 40% of agentic AI projects may be canceled by the end of 2027, citing cost, unclear business value, and inadequate risk controls.These figures show how quickly companies are experimenting with agentic AI. They also make cost, business value, and risk controls increasingly important when deciding where greater autonomy is actually useful.What Brazil reveals about agentic AI adoptionBrazil provides a useful example of how uneven AI adoption can affect the development of agentic products.Cetic.br reported that AI use among Brazilian companies grew from 13% in 2024 to 17% in 2025. The difference by company size was substantial: 50% of large firms used AI, compared with 15% of small firms. Across OECD countries with available data, 52% of large firms used AI in 2025, compared with 17.4% of small firms.AI adoption increased among Brazilian companies from 13% in 2024 to 17% in 2025. In both the Brazil and OECD datasets, reported adoption was higher among large firms. Sources: Cetic.br and OECD. Chart by Lucas Camara.Trust, then, may become a set of interaction primitives: permission, provenance, confirmation, receipt, reversibility, and escalationThe gap matters for UX because an interface can be identical while the conditions behind it are not. One company may have clean data, specialized teams, cloud infrastructure, and mature governance. Another may depend on fragmented records, manual processes, outsourced technology, and little capacity to monitor an agent after launch.In that second environment, token consumption is not an abstract technical detail. It affects which interactions are economically sustainable. A generated analysis may look effortless while requiring repeated model calls, retrieval, validation, and infrastructure that the organization cannot support at scale. A system that depends on perfect data may also fail precisely where automation appears most attractive.Brazil is therefore useful to a global discussion, not as an exception but as an intensified version of a common problem. The OECD describes an emerging AI divide in which larger firms, knowledge-intensive sectors, and more innovative regions move faster. Designing for 2027 means designing across that unevenness, including lower-cost fallbacks, explicit uncertainty, human escalation, and experiences that still work when the agent cannot.For designers, trust can no longer mean only explaining a recommendation. If a system can act, people need to understand what it will do, which information it can access, when it will ask for confirmation, and how an action can be interrupted or reversed.McKinsey’s analysis of the automation curve in agentic commerce makes a useful distinction: delegation is likely to vary according to trust, regret risk, and the value of human involvement. Reordering a familiar product is different from choosing an investment, approving a financial operation, or making a healthcare decision.Regulation is moving in the same direction. Since August 2026, the European Union’s AI Act transparency rules have required people to be informed in certain situations when they are interacting with AI. The European Commission’s Article 50 guidance also addresses machine-readable marking of generated or manipulated content.Trust, then, may become a set of interaction primitives: permission, provenance, confirmation, receipt, reversibility, and escalation.Trust in agentic systems depends on mechanisms that preserve understanding and control before, during, and after an action. Diagram by Lucas Camara.Products may need to work for people and their agentsAnother signal changes the meaning of the word user. Nielsen Norman Group describes AI agents as users, interacting with products alongside people. Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol offers a concrete example of infrastructure designed to let AI surfaces communicate with merchants and perform actions such as checkout.The customer remains human, but a machine may search, compare, interpret, and operate the product before the person sees the final result.This makes structured content, APIs, permissions, error handling, and machine-readable policies part of experience design. A person may never reach a product if their agent cannot understand its information, verify a rule, or complete a task safely.It also creates a new risk. Optimizing only for agents could flatten brands and experiences into whatever is easiest for a machine to compare. Designing only for humans could make the product invisible or unusable in delegated journeys. UX may need to mediate both without forgetting who ultimately lives with the consequence.Research can become faster without becoming automatically betterMy own experiments with website data show both sides of AI-assisted analysis. Connecting analytics and Search Console data can help me identify patterns, profile the real audience of the site, understand how people arrive, and find opportunities for new content. It can bring signals together much faster than reading isolated reports.But a generated persona is not automatically a real person, and a correlation is not an explanation. The output is useful when it helps me ask better questions. It becomes dangerous when a polished synthesis makes assumptions look like evidence.Maze’s Future of User Research Report 2026 found that 69% of researchers were already using AI in their workflows. Respondents still considered interpreting nuance and emotion, making ethical decisions, and framing the right questions areas where human involvement was essential.This matches what I see in practice. AI can help recover information from a call, group data, summarize patterns, and suggest hypotheses. The designer or researcher still needs to know what was lost in the summary, whether the sample supports the claim, and whether the finding makes sense in that specific context.Research may therefore become faster at processing and more demanding at judgment. We will also need to research the AI itself, testing how it behaves across ambiguous requests, incomplete context, conflicting constraints, and failures. A successful happy path tells us very little about a probabilistic system.Design systems are becoming context for machinesI am already seeing the beginning of this discussion in design systems. Teams are exploring Figma and FigJam automation, component generation, and ways to document a system so that an AI agent or MCP integration can understand components, variables, layers, naming, and usage rules.This is close to what I have started testing with Figma’s AI. Layer naming or variable linking can save time, but only when the tool understands enough of the local structure. Without context, automation creates another cleanup task.Figma’s 2026 AI Report, based on 8,403 survey responses and 639 qualitative interviews, found that the boundaries between design and development were already becoming more porous. The share of designers participating in development doubled to 41%, while developers doing design work increased from 44% to 60%.If agents generate interfaces and code, design system documentation must explain more than what a component looks like. It needs to express when the component should be used, what it can contain, how states behave, which accessibility rules are mandatory, and which alternatives should be avoided.Google’s A2UI project makes this direction tangible. Instead of allowing an agent to send arbitrary executable interface code, A2UI lets it describe an interface using components from a catalog controlled by the receiving product. The agent can compose an experience, but the client retains control over rendering, styling, security, and available components.Examples of interfaces composed by AI agents using components from a controlled catalog. Image: Google A2UI TeamComponents become vocabulary. Tokens become constraints. Documentation becomes context. Governance becomes a way to prevent plausible output from drifting away from the product.Does the designer become an auditor?There is an uncomfortable consequence to this shift. If machines generate more screens and states, designers may spend more time reviewing outputs, writing constraints, checking exceptions, and investigating failures. The craft can begin to resemble system auditing.Some of that work is necessary. A probabilistic system cannot be evaluated only through a polished happy path. Someone needs to test ambiguous requests, conflicting permissions, incomplete data, accessibility failures, and actions that cannot easily be reversed. The object of critique expands from a screen to a range of possible behavior.But turning designers into quality control for machine output would be a poor future for the profession. It would place UX at the end of the process again, approving what a model or engineering system has already produced. It would also confuse governance with design.The more useful role begins earlier. Designers can help decide which intentions the system should support, which decisions it may make, what evidence it must expose, what remains stable, and when it must stop and ask a person. Writing agent-readable rules is part of that role, but so are research, framing, prototyping, and the creation of new interaction models.The day-to-day craft may therefore split into two connected activities. One is generative: imagining the relationship between a person and a system that can interpret and act. The other is evaluative: testing whether that relationship remains understandable, inclusive, and accountable across many possible outputs.This is more than prompt writing. A prompt describes a desired response. Product constraints define an operating space. They connect research, policy, data, components, permissions, business rules, and recovery. If designers only polish prompts, the role narrows. If they shape that operating space, the role becomes more consequential.Accessibility cannot be a final check in a generative systemThe WebAIM Million 2026 detected more than 56 million accessibility errors across one million home pages, an average of 56.1 per page. At the same time, the average number of elements on those pages grew 22.5% in one year, reaching 1,437.That relationship between complexity and errors should make us cautious. If AI can generate new states, layouts, controls, and content, accessibility cannot depend on someone reviewing a few predefined screens at the end.It must exist inside the components, constraints, generation rules, automated tests, human evaluation, and monitoring. Accessibility itself is not a trend. What may change is how impossible it becomes to treat it as a static checklist.What the evidence suggests for 2027The signals do not support a world without interfaces. They support interfaces that are more adaptive, conversational, and connected to systems capable of acting.They also show a gap between enthusiasm and maturity. Agent adoption is accelerating while projects are being canceled for cost, weak value, and inadequate controls. Generative interfaces are becoming more capable while expert-designed experiences still outperform them. AI speeds up design and research work while human judgment remains essential for nuance, ethics, and framing.Taken together, these are not separate contradictions. They describe the work ahead.Figma’s State of the Designer 2026 found that 89% of 906 surveyed designers said AI helped them work faster, 80% said it improved collaboration, and 91% said the tools improved their designs. The same report presents craft as a human differentiator.Faster execution does not reduce the need for judgment. It increases the number of possible outputs that someone must evaluate.If a system can create alternatives, UX still needs to decide which problem deserves attention. If it can adapt an interface, UX needs to define what cannot change. If it can act, UX needs to establish permissions, recovery, and accountability. If it can summarize research, UX needs to decide whether the evidence supports the conclusion.By 2027, the role of UX may include drawing fewer predetermined paths and defining more of the boundaries within which a system can create a path. That is still a hypothesis, not a certainty. But it is one that current products, research, standards, and adoption data now make possible to test.The interface will remain important. It just may no longer be the whole experience.References and further readingFigma, State of the Designer 2026. item.title: Neuroqueering design practice
item.description: A look into design as a craft through the lens of neuroqueering.Illustration by Kristina Gushcheva-KeippiläI remember reading Robert Chapman’s Empire of Normality at a strange threshold: in my mid-twenties, a few years into design as a profession, still in a pandemic haze, and on the precipice of what felt like great change. I was discovering a world where fellow neurodivergent thinkers and authors pushed boundaries, revealing a space of possibility beyond the dominant narratives.That rather prolonged period of personal discovery later coincided with a rapid shift in my role toward design leadership. I found myself seeking guidance not solely as a craft expert, but as a not-so-experienced mentor and coach. Fresh into this new reality, I felt a lot of insecurity in my own aptitude to be the design leader I wanted to be, and still need to be. That insecurity manifested itself both as an internal force and as a response to the general state of anxiety amongst designers of the mid-2020s. I still think about this piece by Sara Wachter-Boettcher every day.At times, it was hard for me to connect this personal state of being (a queer, autistic person just trying to figure it out) with my work as a new design leader (a manager and coach really trying to figure it out). But recently, I’ve found even more reinforcement and inspiration in the critical work exploring neurodiversity and queerness. Such work reaffirms and reshapes how we think of our bodyminds, and has plenty to offer to our design practice too.In Neuroqueer Heresies, Dr. Nick Walker introduces “neuroqueering” as a practice of subverting, disrupting, or defying the neuronormative and heteronormative structures. With its roots in Queer Theory, the concept explores how these power structures reinforce each other, and how we may find collective liberation through engaging in interconnected practices that challenge them. The definition is broad, but Dr. Walker sees neuroqueering as an action first.That underlying idea of subversion and transformation is one that I recognise in design itself. To me, design, with its many shapes, has always been just that: a transformative and mediating force between people, technology, and futures.The greatest joy I’ve found in my work recently came from close partnership with fellow design professionals. It’s also come from truly seeing just how much of a changing force design can be, as an inherently explorative discipline which looks forward in time. The paths towards the futures diverge, and there’s nothing more challenging and rewarding than trying to make sense of it as a collective, for the collective.The routes into design can diverge greatly, too. People come from traditional and non-traditional educational backgrounds, shift trades, and learn on their own. Regardless, we share something in common: we want to create and solve something, to make our days as humans lighter or more enriching.Returning to Dr. Walker’s framing of neuroqueering as an action, I wondered if there was a way for me to translate this philosophy into practice that we can employ as designers. To me, the underlying themes are about challenging essentialism, conventional form, and determinism.Original Empire of Normality cover design by David Gee/@davidgeebookdesign (AD: Melanie Patrick). Image edited for this essay.To flourish, we must challenge normalcy and binary thinking. In other words, it means rejecting the idea that there’s a boundary within which our craft must correspond to what the dominant power systems consider the appropriate way to craft a design or experience a design. The neurodiversity paradigm is in direct opposition to the pathology paradigm: the former sees variations of brain function and behaviour as a natural part of human diversity, while the latter perceives neurodivergence as a disorder.Chapman explores this further in Empire of Normality, tracing how the pathology paradigm intertwines with the illusion of normalcy as a scientific, economic, or social truth, a myth that has perpetuated great harm (including but not limited to the popularisation of eugenics and white supremacist rhetoric), especially for marginalised communities.We see the language of marginalisation deeply entrenched in design practice. Consider the term “edge case”, a concept describing a supposedly unlikely scenario of how a person uses a design. When actively employed in craft, such thinking can reinforce our biases and assumptions to varying degrees of exclusion, regardless of intent.In Design for Real Life, Eric Meyer and Sara Wachter-Boettcher reframe “edge cases” as “stress cases”. This shifts the burden away from people experiencing the design towards responsible and considerate action on the part of designers. “Stress case” as a concept communicates urgency, as it highlights how a design may not correspond to the context in which it’s meant to exist.“Dark patterns” is still a widely used metaphoric expression for deceptive, extractive, or simply difficult design patterns — despite it aligning with harmful, anti-Black sentiments which draw parallels between “darkness” and “maliciousness”. Lately, designers have been reaching for “deceptive patterns” as a natural descriptor for such phenomena, which also communicates the concept much more clearly without covering it in metaphor.Language, of course, shapes how we understand our craft, but design as a discipline can also be bound by conventional form. We can understand conventionality as patterns and principles firmly rooted in our understanding of design, be that in its interaction, or in visual presentation. Such forms may be informed by the actions of dominant players in the field, groupthink, or simply trends that seek to benefit the few rather than the craft itself.Determinism, in both what and how we craft, is the antithesis of design. Take for instance the push of AI as an unavoidable technology, one that will embed itself in every facet of our craft. It’s a discourse dominated by the urgency of a conviction: get on board now, or be left behind.We’ve seen it before. Technology changes. Because design is a mediating force, its core is about building a deeper understanding and connection between our craft and the world it inhabits. Such determinism forces us to teach each other the wrong lesson: that our craft’s worth amounts to speed over reflection, or tool prowess over judgement and intentionality.This year, my team and I have worked on formulating what great design means to us. Although we’ve been working together for months, years in some cases, we hadn’t really stopped, together, to build consensus around what great design actually is. Our conversations were revealing: alongside human-centricity, reflection, and delight, we kept returning to systems-thinking as the thread that ties great design together.Each principle plays its own part in our philosophy. Systems-thinking specifically raises an interesting duality: convention can be both a guideline and a signal for change. Systems change. We want to abstract and extend the conventions that work, but remain alert to the parts of a system that create barriers or mismatches in experience. That’s where we complement systems-thinking with design that centres people, that is in dialogue with its context, and that seeks moments of lightness and joy.To me, this is what neuroqueering design practice is: the radical idea that there is no normalcy, that how we do design and what we design are subject to exploration and subversion, to design for people, for dignity, and for purpose.Kristina (she/they) is a design leader based in Finland. Kristina writes about inclusive design, being autistic at work, and thinking in systems.Acknowledgements and referencesThanks to Rae, Jenni, and my team for helping this piece see the light of day. ❤Robert Chapman: Empire of Normalityhttps://www.plutobooks.com/product/empire-of-normality/Sara Wachter-Boettcher: Hey designers, they’re gaslighting you.https://medium.com/nice-work-from-active-voice/hey-designers-theyre-gaslighting-you-e02e5a4d9cffNick Walker: Neuroqueer Heresieshttps://neuroqueer.com/neuroqueer-heresies/National Autistic Society: Autism and neurodiversityhttps://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/identity/autism-and-neurodiversity#What%20is%20the%20neurodiversity%20paradigm?Eric Meyer, Sara Wachter-Boettcher: Design for Real Lifehttps://abookdeparts-dfrl.netlify.app/Intuit: Anti-racist languagehttps://contentdesign.intuit.com/accessibility-and-inclusion/anti-racist-language/Neuroqueering design practice was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
